keyframes.prompt: Vertical 2:3 realistic photo of a cut-away view of a red imported fire ant nest under a sunny lawn, seen from the side at ground level, like a clean vertical slice through the ground. The upper 30 percent of the frame: green lawn grass and a bright blue sky with soft white clouds. At the horizontal center, a dome-shaped fire ant mound of loose, crumbly, light-brown soil rises from the grass; the mound has no hole on top. The lower 70 percent of the frame: the cut face of moist dark-brown soil under the mound, with small stones and fine grass roots, and a network of narrow tunnels and small rounded chambers going down from the mound. Tiny reddish-brown worker ants walk in some tunnels, and some chambers hold small white heaps of ant brood. At the horizontal center of the frame, at 70 percent of the frame height, is one larger flat oval chamber, a little brighter than the others. Inside it rests one large dark fire ant queen beside a tiny heap of white eggs. Soft daylight falls on the cut face of the soil from the front. Realistic photo, natural colors, deep focus, not a diagram, not an illustration. Keep everything important away from the left and right edges. No people. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. The camera has moved forward and down into the larger oval chamber at the center of the cut-away soil. Show a close-up of the inside of this one chamber, seen from the side at the level of its floor. The chamber is a smooth flat oval cavity in moist dark-brown soil, wider than tall, in the middle of the frame; its floor is a gentle curve at 62 percent of the frame height. Dark soil with small stones and fine roots fills the frame above and below the chamber. A narrow tunnel leaves the chamber at its upper left. The same soft daylight falls on the cut face from the front, so the chamber is clearly lit and the soil around it is a little darker. On the chamber floor, just left of the frame center, rests one large wingless fire ant queen (Solenopsis invicta), seen from the side, her body horizontal with her head to the left: reddish-brown head and thorax with small wing scars, elbowed antennae, six legs, and a large swollen glossy dark-brown abdomen. Her body is about one quarter of the frame width long, and the tip of her abdomen is just left of the horizontal center. Right next to the tip of her abdomen, at the horizontal center of the frame, lies a small heap of about five tiny glossy white oval eggs; each egg is one twelfth as long as the queen. Keep the queen and the eggs within the middle 60 percent of the frame width. Only one ant. Macro photo, sharp focus on the queen and the eggs. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the chamber, the soil, the tunnel, the lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The queen stays in exactly the same place, pose and size. The heap of tiny white eggs next to her abdomen stays in the same place, but it is now three times bigger, with about fifteen eggs of the same size. Only one ant. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the chamber, the soil, the tunnel, the lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The queen stays in exactly the same place, pose and size. The eggs have hatched: in exactly the same place lies a small heap of about twelve tiny newly hatched larvae, each soft, translucent milky-white and curved like a comma, a little bigger than an egg, about one ninth as long as the queen. No eggs left. Only one adult ant. No text, no watermark.

The larvae stay in the same place next to her abdomen, at the horizontal center of the frame, but there are now about ten larvae and each is three times longer than now: plump, pearly white, curved gourd-shaped grubs, thicker at the rear, with a small head at the narrow front end. Keep the heap within the middle 60 percent of the frame width. Only one adult ant. No text, no watermark.
